question:
Patient note:
A 68-year-old man with a decade-long history of ischemic cardiomyopathy complicated by reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (most recently 35 % on an outpatient echocardiogram six months ago) and chronic New York Heart Association class II symptoms arrived at the emergency department just after noon complaining of two days of foul-smelling, jet-black bowel movements that required repeated flushing to clear the bowl, the latest occurring an hour before arrival and noted to cling to the porcelain with a tar-like consistency. He stated he had felt increasingly fatigued and mildly light-headed when climbing the stairs from his basement workshop but never experienced spinning, tunnel vision, or loss of consciousness and was able to drive himself to the hospital without incident. He denied vomiting, retching, passage of bright red blood per rectum, chest pain, palpitations beyond his usual awareness of an irregular beat from occasional premature contractions, cough, fever, or abdominal distention. Daily medications include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg every morning, furosemide 40 mg each morning with a potassium chloride supplement, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and low-dose aspirin 81 mg for secondary prevention after a drug-eluting stent placed three years prior; he has not used nonsteroidal anti-inflammatories since a gastroenterologist advised against them and has never been prescribed oral anticoagulants. He reports adherence to a 2-gram sodium diet, restricts fluid to 1.5 L per day, and weighs himself each morning, noting no abrupt change this week. He quit smoking twelve years ago after a 25-pack-year history and drinks one or two light beers on weekends. There is no family history of bleeding disorders or upper gastrointestinal malignancy. On arrival he was seated upright on the gurney, skin appearing pale and slightly cool but dry, conversing in full sentences and oriented to person, place, and time. Triage vital signs obtained prior to intravenous access documented blood pressure 117/70 mm Hg in the right arm at heart level, regular pulse 89 beats per minute by automated monitor, respirations 18 per minute, oral temperature 36.9 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing ambient air. Jugular venous pulsation measured 7 cm H₂O with the head of the bed at 45°, peripheral pulses were symmetric though slightly diminished, and capillary refill was under three seconds. Cardiac auscultation revealed a displaced, diffuse apical impulse and an S3 gallop without new murmurs; lungs were clear at the apices with faint bibasilar crackles that resolved after the patient sat forward. Abdomen was flat, soft, and mildly tender in the epigastrium without guarding, rebound, palpable masses, or organomegaly; bowel sounds were hyperactive. No spider angiomata, palmar erythema, scleral icterus, or asterixis was observed. Lower extremities showed trace pitting edema at the ankles, unchanged from his baseline per the patient. Digital rectal examination produced a generous smear of shiny, pitch-black material that rapidly turned the guaiac card dark blue. Neurologic screening demonstrated intact cranial nerves, full strength, and normal finger-to-nose testing; tandem gait was not assessed because the patient preferred to remain seated after the rectal exam. Two 16-gauge peripheral intravenous catheters were placed after blood specimens were drawn, but no crystalloid, diuretic, proton-pump inhibitor, vasoactive infusion, or transfusion had yet been administered. Initial laboratory results, all obtained before any treatment, revealed hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, hematocrit 35 %, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, platelet count 226 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.8 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 36 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.1 mg/dL), sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 92 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 28 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 25 U/L, albumin 3.8 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.08. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained in triage showed normal sinus rhythm at 88 bpm with left ventricular hypertrophy pattern and no acute ischemic change. Upright chest radiograph demonstrated mild cardiomegaly consistent with known history, clear lung fields, and no free subdiaphragmatic air. Supine abdominal film displayed a nonspecific gas pattern. Type and screen were sent for cross-match, the patient was kept nil per os, placed on continuous cardiac telemetry, and the gastroenterology service was paged for urgent endoscopic evaluation of the suspected upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses pretreatment laboratory values, vital signs, presenting symptoms, and comorbidities:
- BUN 36 mg/dL corresponds to urea 12.9 mmol/L (10 to <25 mmol/L) = 4.
- Hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL in a man (10 to <12 g/dL) = 3.
- Systolic BP 117 mmHg (≥110) = 0.
- Pulse 89/min (<100) = 0.
- Melena: black, tarry stool confirmed on examination = 1.
- Syncope: light-headedness without loss of consciousness = 0.
- Hepatic disease: none documented = 0.
- Heart failure: chronic symptomatic cardiomyopathy with LVEF 35% = 2, even though clinically stable.
Total: 4 + 3 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 10.
Final answer: 10
